induced samples could be expanded. It would be valuable to clarify the similarities and
differences in cell composition and pathway activity between the two conditions,
particularly considering how closely 20E treatment mimics natural developmental
processes.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. We agree
that a detailed comparison between natural development and 20E-induced conditions is
essential for evaluating the fidelity of the hormone induction system. To address this
point, we expanded our analyses of both cellular composition and pathway activity in
the revised manuscript.
At the cellular level, the major cell types captured in both conditions were similar.
However, their relative abundances and activation timings were different. During
natural development, the proportions of Wm, Cuticle, and Epithelial lineages changed
gradually from L5D1 to W1. In contrast, 20E treatment triggered a rapid and transient
expansion of these lineages within the first 30 min, followed by a pronounced shift
toward Matrix and Immune cell enrichment after 40 min. Notably, Matrix cells
exhibited a steady increase in both conditions (Fig. S18a).
At the transcriptional level, GO and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed distinct
functional states. Natural development (sc group) showed enrichment in Endocytosis,
mTOR signaling pathway, structural constituent of cuticle, and DNA-binding
transcription factor binding, reflecting sustained biosynthetic and morphogenetic
activity. Conversely, 20E-induced samples (sn group) were enriched in Ribosome
binding, mRNA binding, and Oxidative phosphorylation, indicating enhanced protein
synthesis, energy metabolism, and rapid transcriptional reprogramming (Fig. S18b–c).
These findings demonstrate that 20E treatment recapitulates the natural developmental
trajectory but in a time-compressed manner, accelerating lineage activation and
transcriptional remodeling. We have included these results in the revised manuscript
(Page 13, Lines 326–337) and added Supplementary Fig. S18 to clarify these
comparisons.
Comment: 3. For Fig. S17, please provide functional enrichment results for the shared
upregulated gene set between the natural and 20E-induced groups. This would help
clarify the core biological processes directly regulated by 20E.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. According to
your suggestion, we performed Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway enrichment
analyses on the 273 shared upregulated genes identified in both the natural development
and 20E-induced datasets. The enrichment results revealed that these shared genes are
significantly involved in developmental processes such as cellular morphogenesis,
organ growth, and tissue remodeling, as well as in stress and immune responses. In
addition, several pathways related to protein homeostasis and signal transduction—
including autophagy, MAPK signaling, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) protein
processing—were also enriched. These findings suggest that 20E regulates a core
transcriptional program that coordinates both structural remodeling and cellular stress
adaptation during wing disc development (Fig. S19b). We also analyzed the dynamic
expression patterns of these shared genes across natural development and 20E-treated
samples (Fig. S19c). The results showed a progressive, stage-specific activation from
L5D1 to P6 under natural development, transitioning sequentially from clusters C1 to
C10. Upon 20E treatment, many genes in clusters C3–C6 and C8–C10 responded
rapidly within 20 minutes, while genes in cluster C1, which were activated early during
natural development, were induced later under 20E exposure. These observations
provide a high-resolution view of 20E-induced transcriptional reprogramming and
underscore its role in accelerating developmental transitions within the wing disc. We
have incorporated these analyses into the revised Supplementary Figure S19 and
updated the corresponding description in the main text (Page 14, Lines 337–353). The
legend of Fig. S19 has also been revised accordingly.
Comment: 4. In Fig. 4h–i, the analysis of cell–cell interactions (CCI) does not clearly
reflect stage-specific dynamics. The authors are encouraged to highlight temporal shifts
in interaction patterns across developmental stages.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s careful work. We fully agree that highlighting
the stage-specific dynamics of cell–cell interactions (CCIs) would make the results
more intuitive. Accordingly, we revised and expanded the CCI analysis to better
illustrate temporal changes in intercellular communication across the five
developmental stages. In the revised version, we visualized the overall interaction
networks for each stage and emphasized their dynamic complexity (Fig. 4l). The cell-
cell interaction network gradually became more complex from Stage 1 to Stage 4 and
then simplified at Stage 5, indicating a transition from active remodeling to stabilization
(Fig. 4l). To improve clarity, we restructured Figs. 4m-n by highlighting the main
signaling sources with bold text and labeling each stage-specifically enriched
interactions with the corresponding stage label. This presentation makes the temporal
pattern of CCIs and the stage-specific signaling hubs easier to follow and interpret.
Please see Figure 4 for the revised visualization. The corresponding explanations have
been added to the main text of the revised manuscript (Page 17-19, Lines 414–448).
Comment: 5. The adult wing morphology following Rfx RNAi in Spodoptera
frugiperda is not shown. Including representative images of adult wing phenotypes
would strengthen the phenotypic validation. Given its importance in supporting the
evolutionary conservation of Rfx, the S. frugiperda RNAi results should be moved to
the main figures. Additionally, a comparative analysis of Rfx conservation across
insects would further support this claim.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important and constructive
suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have added representative images of the adult
wing phenotypes in S. frugiperda following Rfx RNAi to Figure 2 (Fig. 2o and Page
10, Line 231).
These images clearly display the morphological defects, such as shortened veins
and irregular wing margins, which support the functional disruption of Rfx. To highlight
the evolutionary conservation of Rfx, we have moved the Rfx RNAi knock down results
of S. frugiperda from the Supplementary Materials to the main figures (Fig. 2m–n).
Furthermore, to strengthen the evidence for evolutionary conservation, we
performed a comparative analysis of Rfx orthologs across representative insect species.
We constructed a phylogenetic tree using Rfx protein sequences from 23 representative
insect species and examined their motif organization and conserved domain
architecture. The analysis revealed that Rfx is highly conserved across Lepidoptera and
other insect lineages, suggesting a conserved regulatory function in wing development
(Fig. S10). Please see Supplementary Figure S10 below for the phylogenetic and motif
analyses. These new results and corresponding figure have been incorporated into the
revised manuscript (Supplementary Fig. S10 and Page 9, Lines 220–222). The
legends for Fig. 2 and Fig. S10 have also been updated accordingly.
Supplementary Fig. 10 Conservation and evolutionary analysis of Rfx. a Phylogenetic analysis
of Rfx orthologs in representative insects. b Conserved motif architecture of Rfx proteins. c Domain
composition of Rfx proteins based on CDD annotation.
Comment: 6. Beyond Rfx, the authors are encouraged to functionally validate
additional key transcription factors identified through SCENIC analysis (e.g., Dll or
Blimp-1) via RNAi or similar approaches.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. In the revised manuscript,
we have included additional functional validation experiments for key transcription
factors identified through the SCENIC analysis. Specifically, we focused on Distal-less
(Dll) and Pur-alpha, both predicted to play central roles in Wm cell differentiation and
wing disc development. RNAi-mediated knockdown of these genes in Bombyx mori
resulted in noticeable morphological defects in the wing disc, confirming their essential
regulatory roles in morphogenesis (Fig. S11). Please see Supplementary Figure S11
below. As for Blimp-1, previous studies have reported that RNAi-mediated knockdown
of Blimp-1 in Bombyx mori leads to disrupted wing development (Wu SY et al., 2019)1.
This literature evidence supports the functional importance of Blimp-1 identified in our
analysis and further exemplify the reliability of our transcription factor (TF) screening
strategy. Together, these results provide additional support for the functional relevance
of the key TFs identified by SCENIC. The new experimental results and related
references have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Fig. S11 and Page 9,
Lines 225–228).
Supplementary Fig. 11 Effects of dll and pur-α gene knockdown on larval wing discs and adult
wing development in silkworm. a qPCR analysis of gene changes after Dll and Pur-α genes
interference, Data represented by the mean ± SD, were analyzed for intergroup comparison using
unpaired t-tests, with significance at **, p < 0.01. b Morphological changes in wing discs of
silkworn after Dll and Pur-α genes knockdown, showing developmental fissures and defects.
Bright-field imaging revealed the overall tissue architecture. Phalloidin staining labeled actin
filaments to visualize cytoskeletal organization. DAPI staining marked nuclear DNA for cellular
localization. Merged images integrated Phalloidin and DAPI signals to delineate spatial
relationships between cytoskeletal elements and nuclei. c Knockdown of Dll and Pur-α genes
resulted in atrophy and malformation of wing development in adult silkworm. Dll knockdown
induced wing atrophy with reduced size, Pur-α knockdown led to morphological distortions in adult
wings.
Comment: 7. In Fig. 3g, it would be helpful to indicate which cell types express the
highlighted transcription factors and how their activity contributes to cell-type-specific
transcriptional regulation and heterogeneity.
Response: We thank the reviewers for pointing out this issue. According to your
suggestion, we have provided the cell-type–specific expression patterns and temporal
activities of the transcription factors in Supplementary Figure S16a. Based on regulon
specificity scores (RSS) and expression dynamics across developmental stages, we
identified six key TFs that exhibit distinct temporal activation patterns and cell-type
preferences. In the early stage (before 30 min), Hr38 (LOC693064), Nubbin
(LOC101744796), and Six2 (LOC101735990) showed strong activity, regulating gene
networks enriched in Wm, Epithelial 1, and Cuticle 1 cells. After 30 min, CREB
(LOC692871), FoxN3 (LOC101739133), and GATA-A (LOC10174013) became
predominant, with activities mainly associated with Immune and Matrix cells. These
findings suggest a temporal transition of TF activity from early patterning factors to
regulators of morphogenesis and tissue remodeling. We have incorporated these
analyses and explanatory descriptions into the revised manuscript (Figs. 3g and S16,
Page 12, Lines 304–312), and the legends of Fig. 3g and Fig. S16 have been updated
accordingly.
Comment: 8. The evolutionary comparison with Drosophila and B. anynana is
relatively brief. A more detailed discussion of conserved and lineage-specific
developmental strategies across these species would enhance the impact of the
comparative analysis.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree
that a deeper evolutionary perspective would enhance the impact of our comparative
analysis. Comparing our findings in B. mori with that of D. melanogaster and B.
anynana revealed both conserved regulatory modules and lineage-specific
developmental strategies (Fig. S23a and b). Core pathways such as Wnt, Notch, and
MAPK were consistently involved in cell fate determination and tissue patterning
across species. However, our findings highlight several specific adaptations in B. mori.
Specifically, the Wm cell in B. mori followed a bifurcated developmental trajectory
toward epithelial and cuticle fates. This distinct progenitor identity has not been clearly
reported in Drosophila, suggesting a silkworm-specific mechanism for lineage
allocation. In B. anynana, a more diversified set of scale precursor cells supports
elaborate wing coloration and patterning, highlighting another lineage-specific
adaptation (Fig. S23c). Furthermore, although 20E functions as a conserved hormone
regulating metamorphosis, our data point to a silkworm-specific mode of spatial and
temporal hormone responsiveness. In B. mori, Wm cells responded rapidly and locally
to 20E, initiating early morphogenetic programs. This contrasts with the more systemic
and less spatially resolved 20E response observed in Drosophila. Taken together, these
comparisons demonstrate that while fundamental signaling frameworks are preserved,
each lineage has evolved tailored regulatory strategies—shaped by ecological pressures
and morphogenetic needs. Our single-cell and spatial atlas of B. mori not only confirms
these shared principles but also provides a valuable reference for exploring how
evolutionary flexibility in hormone integration and progenitor dynamics contributes to
wing diversity in insects. We have expanded the Discussion section to include this
detailed comparison in the revised manuscript (Pages 23-24, Lines 554–572).
Comment: 9. While the methods section is generally well-detailed, additional
clarification on the threshold settings and statistical parameters used in transcription
factor enrichment, module identification, and pathway analysis would improve
transparency and reproducibility.
Response: We thank the reviewer's careful work. We have thoroughly gone through the
Methods section and revise accordingly. To be specific, we have added detailed
descriptions of the threshold settings and statistical parameters used in transcription
factor enrichment, gene module identification, and pathway enrichment analysis. In
addition, we have further included important methodological details to enhance
transparency and reproducibility, such as catalog numbers of key reagents, names and
version of software, database sources, and parameter configurations used throughout
the analyses. These additions have been incorporated into the revised Methods section
(Pages 25–31).
Comment: 10. Below are some minor comments for the authors to consider: In Fig. 2j,
the figure legend should specify “dsRfx” to match the experimental description. The
labels in Fig. 3a–f should be adjusted for better alignment, and the RSS values in Fig.
3j are too small to read clearly and should be enlarged.
Response: We thank the reviewers for pointing out this issue. All suggested corrections
have been implemented in the revised manuscript and figure, including but not limited
to: “dsRfx” has been added to the legend of Fig. 2j to accurately reflect the experimental
condition; the labels in Fig. 3a–f have been realigned for improved clarity and visual
consistency; the RSS values in Fig. 3j have been enlarged to enhance readability. These
modifications have been incorporated into the revised figures and corresponding
legends (Page 10, line 231 and Page 15, line 354).
Comment: 11. Several supplementary figures appear to lack sufficient resolution.
Please ensure all images are high-quality and include appropriate legends and
annotations for ease of interpretation.
Response: Thank you for your careful review. We have addressed this concern by
adjusting the resolution of all supplementary figures to ensure high-quality
visualization. In addition, we have thoroughly checked the entire manuscript and
supplementary materials to confirm that all images are of sufficient resolution (>300
dpi) and include clear legends and annotations for ease of interpretation. Please see the
revised Supplementary data with changes marked.
Comment: 12. Reference formatting should be carefully reviewed. Inconsistencies in
journal name abbreviations and missing page numbers should be corrected for
uniformity.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. We have carefully
reviewed and standardized the reference formatting throughout the manuscript to
ensure full consistency. Please see the revised manuscript with changes marked.
Comment: 13. In the author list, a comma should follow “Ying Lin” to maintain
consistent punctuation.
Response: We thank the reviewer's careful work. We have corrected the punctuation
by adding a comma after “Ying Lin” to ensure consistency in the author list (Page 1,
line 6).
Comment: 14. Line 27: The full name of 20E should be written as “20-
hydroxyecdysone”.
Response: Thank you for your careful review. We have revised the text to spell out the
full name of 20E as “20-hydroxyecdysone” (Page 1, line 26).
Comment: 15. Line 90: “Fig. S1” should include a period to follow journal formatting
guidelines.
Response: We thank the reviewer's careful work. We have corrected the formatting
issue by adding a period to “Fig. S1” (Page 3, line 93).
Comment: 16. Lines 105–106: The font style of reference citations appears
inconsistent (non-italic). Please standardize formatting across the manuscript.
Response: Thank you for your careful work. We have corrected the font style of the
reference citations (Page 4, line 106). Additionally, we have reviewed the entire
manuscript to standardize reference formatting throughly.
Comment: 17. Lines 180 and 185: The correct formatting should be “Fig. 2f and Fig.
S7c”.
Response: We thank the reviewers for pointing out this issue. We have corrected the
formatting in Lines 180 and 185 to “Fig. 2f and Fig. S7c” (Page 8, line 192). We have
also carefully reviewed the entire manuscript to ensure that all figure references follow
consistent and proper formatting.
Reference
1. Wu SY, et al. BmBlimp-1 gene encoding a C2H2 zinc finger protein is required
for wing development in the silkworm Bombyx mori. Int J Biol Sci 15, 2664-
2675 (2019).
Reviewer #2
Comment: 1. The current manuscript outlines a spatial transcriptomic approach to map
the development of wing discs in Bombyx mori. The authors have compiled an
impressive dataset, and undertaken extensive analysis, to identify the cell types within
this tissue, their spatial location, the changes in cell fates over time, and changes in gene
expression that accompany these changes. In addition, they explore how the steroid
hormone ecdysone affects wing disc development, demonstrating that it regulates the
pace of wing disc development. We commend the authors on the scale of this work, and
feel that it makes a valuable contribution to our understanding of organ development.
We have no experience with the transcriptomics approaches used and thus will limit our
comments to other aspects of the work, which we think would help strengthen the
manuscript.
Response: We deeply appreciate the respected reviewer for their meticulous
examination and valuable suggestions on our manuscript. According to your
suggestions, we have made extensive modifications to our manuscript and
supplemented extra data to make our results convincing. Thank you again for your
positive comments and valuable suggestions to improve the quality of our manuscript.
Comment: 2. The acronyms for the different cell types are really hard to keep track of.
Can you use the whole word to make it easier to follow?
Response: We thank the reviewers for pointing out this issue. We fully understand that
the numerous acronyms may be difficult to follow. To improve clarity and readability,
we have carefully revised the text and figures to ensure that all abbreviations are clearly
defined and consistently explained.
In our study, due to the large number of cell types identified through single-cell
analysis, we adopted standard practice by using abbreviations (e.g., Wm for wing
morphogenesis, Im for immune, etc.) to enhance figure readability and minimize label
overcrowding. Nonetheless, we fully recognize the importance of clarity. Therefore, we
have adopted the following strategy:
For cell types with longer or more complex names (e.g., wing morphogenesis), we
use abbreviations such as “Wm” to simplify figure labels while maintaining readability.
For short or self-explanatory names (e.g., Cuticle 1–3), we now use the full terms
instead of abbreviations.
For figure clarity and layout efficiency, some figures are abbreviated as needed;
all abbreviations are defined in the corresponding figure legends.
In addition, we have carefully revised all figures, figure legends, and relevant parts
of the main text to ensure that all abbreviations are clearly defined and explained at first
mention. We have also added explicit acronym-to-full-name mappings. All related
figures, legends, and relevant text sections have been carefully updated to maintain
consistency. Please see the revised manuscript for these modifications with changes
marked.
Comment: 3. The experiments knocking down Rfx in the wing disc were very
interesting and highlighted the role of this gene in Wing Morphogenesis cell type
development. However, it wasn’t clear why this particular cell type was the focus?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful question. Our focus on
the Wing Morphogenesis (Wm) cell type was based on several layers of observations
during wing disc (WD) development.
First, when examining the dynamic changes in the proportion and differentiation
trajectory of cell types across developmental stages, we observed that most cell types
in the WD maintained a relatively stable state and did not exhibit significant lineage
progression (as shown in Fig. S6a–f). In contrast, Wm cells demonstrated a markedly
dynamic and continuous differentiation trajectory, with clear transitions toward cuticle
and epithelial (EP) lineages (Fig. S6g). This suggests that Wm cells are a pivotal cell
type in the developmental progression of the wing disc. Second, spatial transcriptomics
data further corroborated this finding. We identified Wm cells as being specifically
enriched in the wing bud region, the future wing-forming domain of the WD (Fig. 1g–
h). This spatial localization aligns with their predicted role in driving the formation of
wing-specific structures. Motivated by the above observations, we sought to uncover
potential transcriptional regulators specifically involved in wing disc cell fate decisions.
Through the reconstruction of a transcription factor regulatory network and RSS
scoring, we found that Rfx emerged as the top-ranked specific transcription factor at
the L5D1 stage. Which leading us to hypothesize that Rfx may serve as a core regulator
in Wm cell lineage commitment.
To validate this hypothesis, we performed RNAi-mediated knockdown of Rfx and
observed striking disruptions in wing disc morphology and gene expression associated
with Wm-derived lineages (Fig. 2j–l and Fig. S9), confirming its critical role in
modulating Wm cell fate and wing development.
Comment: 4. This might sound a bit picky, but the order of the methods did not follow
the order of experiments. This isn’t necessary, but does help when trying to find the
relevant method to match to the experiment.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree that
organizing the Methods section to follow the experimental sequence described in the
Results enhances readability and makes it easier for readers to locate relevant
methodological details. To address this, we have reordered the Methods subsections in
the revised manuscript to match the chronological flow of experiments presented in the
main text—from sample collection and sequencing, through data processing and
analyses, to functional validation and hormone treatment assays. Please see the revised
Methods section (pages 25–31) in the revised manuscript.
Comment: 5. For the wing disc culture experiments, more detail is required in the
methods to understand how these were performed. What medium did you use for
culture and did you add any insulin or bovine serum? Preferably, this would have it’s
own section. For the experimental design, why did you choose to change the time of
exposure instead of 20E dose? Lastly, 2µg / ml of 20E is a high dose for wing disc
cultures. It would be useful to explain why you chose this dose.
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. We have added a dedicated
section in the Methods to comprehensively describe the in vitro wing disc culture and
20E treatment experiments. Specifically, the wing discs were cultured in Grace’s
medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum.
Regarding the experimental design, we chose to vary the duration of 20E exposure
rather than its concentration. This decision was based on two main considerations. First,
due to the open circulatory system of Bombyx mori, endogenous 20E levels in the
hemolymph can influence multiple tissues simultaneously. Second, the permeability
and uptake efficiency of exogenous 20E by the wing disc in vitro is unclear. This
approach allowed us to capture the temporal sequence of gene activation in response to
20E and to compare it with the natural developmental timeline.
To ensure a robust and consistent hormonal response will be induced in cultured
wing discs, we performed a preliminary dose-response experiment to select optimized
concentration for 20E. Wing discs were cultured with various concentrations of 20E (0,
0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, and 10 μg/mL) and relative expression of key 20E responsive genes
were measured using quantitative PCR. We found that at 2 µg/mL, the transcriptional
levels of EcR and USP, were markedly induced (Fig. S13a). This concentration is also
supported by previous studies reporting effective hormonal stimulation at similar levels
in cultured wing discs (Ali et al., 2019)1. Hence, we used 2 µg/mL 20E to stimulate
wing disc in vitro to investigate gene expression dynamics. All these details have been
incorporated into the revised Methods section (Page 11 lines 266–269 and pages 28-
29 lines 707–730).
Supplementary Fig. 13 Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) analysis of 20E treated
wing disc. a Changes in relative expression levels of EcR and USP genes in wing discs after 4 h of
in vitro culture under different concentrations of 20E hormone. b UMAP plots showing the
distribution of different cell types at various time points (0 min–6 h). c Temporal changes in the
proportions of different cell types. d The proportion of time point-specific upregulated genes in
different cell types.
Comment: 6. Why were 20E titres collected from the wing discs and not from the
hemolymph?
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful question. We chose to analyze 20E titers
directly from the wing discs (WDs) rather than the hemolymph for the following
reasons. First, the dynamic changes of 20E concentration in the hemolymph during
silkworm development have already been well documented in previous studies. Second,
the silkworm possesses an open circulatory system, and 20E in the hemolymph is
distributed to various tissues and organs, not exclusively acting on the wing discs.
Therefore, measuring 20E in the hemolymph would not provide precise information
about the local hormonal milieu experienced by the developing WDs. Our goal was to
investigate the tissue-specific 20E dynamics during wing morphogenesis, and thus we
directly measured the hormone levels in the WDs. We have clarified this rationale in
the Method section of revised manuscript to improve transparency (Page 30, line 774–
778).
Comment: 7. Some of the paragraphs were in really big blocks of text. It would help
with readability to break up these paragraphs into discrete ideas and to provide a bit
more context throughout with regards to the aims of your different analyses.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. We have broken up the
long paragraphs into shorter, focused units and added brief contextual sentences to
clarify the purpose of each analysis, improving overall readability and flow. Please see
the version of revised manuscript with changes marked.
Comment: 8. Minor comments: Line 38-39: not all insects have wing discs
(ametabolous and hemimetabolous insects have wing buds which are analogous)
Response: We thank the reviewer's careful work. To address this, we have revised the
sentence to clarify that wing discs are specific to holometabolous insects (Page 2,
lines 38-39).
Comment: 9. Line 48-50: Rephrase this sentence as it sounds like you are saying that
Bicyclus anynana is not a lepidopteran.
Response: We agree that the original sentence may unintentionally imply that Bicyclus
anynana is not a lepidopteran. We have revised the sentence as “Although single-cell
analyses have been conducted for the wing disc of Drosophila melanogaster (D. melanogaster)
and Bicyclus anynana (B. anynana), they have mainly focused on cell type composition and
gene expression patterns at isolated stages.”, to improve clarity and accuracy (Page 2, lines
48–50).
Comment: 10. Figure 2K legend: what do the arrowheads point to? Also, there are two
sets of dsEGFP and two sets of dsRfx panels. How are these different?
Response: We greatly appreciate your attention to this detail. We apologize for the lack
of clarity in the original figure legend. The arrowheads in Figure 2K highlight regions
of morphological changes in the wing disc before and after RNAi treatment (Page 11,
Lines 245–252). As for the two sets of dsEGFP and dsRfx panels: they represent the
same experimental groups but illustrate different levels of observation. The upper
panels display the overall morphology of the wing discs. The lower panels show
transverse histological sections of the same samples, allowing visualization of
structural differences in tissue organization and cellular morphology after RNAi
treatment. We have revised both Figure 2 and its legend to clarify this distinction (Fig.
2 and Page 11, Lines 246–248).
Comment: 11. Line 242: You mention Usp is expressed in Wm cells, but EcR isn’t in
the list of ecdysone response genes?
Response: We thank the reviewer’s careful work. We found that EcR gene expression
was barely detected in our snRNA-seq dataset. This might be due to stochastic dropout
events, arising from the limited RNA content in single cell nucleus and inefficiencies
of capture and reverse transcription steps during snRNA-seq experiment (Kharchenko
et al., 2014)2. As a result, transcripts expressed at low abundance or in a transient
manner are often not detected, even when they are biologically present in the cell. After
20E treatment, we observed that Usp gene have a higher expression level than EcR
gene, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 13a above. This might explain why Usp
expression was sufficiently robust to be captured during the experiment, whereas EcR
may have been underrepresented due to such stochastic dropout effects.
Comment: 12. In the text, you refer to 12 supplementary tables. These tables are found
in the excel file. However, in the pdf there are only 3 supplementary tables and the
formatting of these tables appears to be off.
Response: Thank you for your careful work. We sincerely apologize for the confusion
caused by the inconsistency between the number of supplementary tables and those
included in the PDF. This has now been corrected: all 12 supplementary tables are
properly provided in the updated Excel file, and the PDF version has been revised to
include the appropriate references and formatting. We would also like to note that the
supplementary tables were intentionally not converted into PDF format for
resubmission. Due to the layout and data density of these tables, conversion may cause
display or formatting issues when generating the integrated manuscript PDF. We have
explained this to the editor in advance and clarified that all supplementary tables are
provided as separate Excel files to ensure clarity and accessibility of the data. Please
see the revised supplementary tables.
Comment: 13. For Figure 3d (and the accompanying supplementary figure), it wasn’t
clear what was meant by relative information flow.
Response: We thank the reviewers for pointing out this issue. We have clarified the
meaning of “relative information flow” in the revised version of Figure 3d legend and
the associated supplementary figure 14a legend. Specifically, it refers to the normalized
strength and direction of ligand–receptor–mediated signaling interactions among cell
types, inferred based on gene expression profiles and prior knowledge of ligand–
receptor pairs. Please see page 15 lines 361–363 in the revised manuscript.
Comment: 14. Figure S18: What do BF and Trans refer to?
Response: We thank the reviewers for pointing out this issue. We have clarified the
meaning of this abbreviation in the revised figure legend. Specifically, “BF” has been
clarified as Bright field, and “Trans” as Transverse section (Fig. S20 and Page 11, lines
245-251). All relevant instances in the figure have been updated accordingly.
Reference:
1. Ali MS, Mishra B, Swapon AH, Yamaguchi M. Successively expressed cuticular protein genes
at the prepupal stage in wing discs of Bombyx mori. The Journal of Basic and Applied Zoology
80, (2019).
2. Peter V Kharchenko, Lev Silberstein, David T Scadden. Bayesian approach to single-cell
differential expression analysis. Nat Methods 11, 740–742 (2014)
Reviewer #3
Comment: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the
listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training
in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who
co-review manuscripts.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their contribution as a co-reviewer and
for taking the time to evaluate our manuscript. We truly appreciate your effort and
thoughtful participation in the review process.
Your collaborative review, along with the feedback provided by the other
reviewers, has been highly constructive and has helped us substantially improve the
clarity, structure, and scientific rigor of our study.
We have carefully addressed all comments and incorporated the suggested
revisions throughout the manuscript. Please see the detailed point-by-point responses
above for the corresponding changes.
Response to reviewers
We deeply appreciate the respected reviewer for thier very professional
comments and suggestions, which help us to improve the quality of the manuscript
significantly!

## Paper

## Abstract

Insect wing development involves tissue patterning, cell fate transitions, and hormone signaling, yet its spatiotemporal logic remains unclear. The silkworm, with large wing discs and defined stages, provides an ideal model for high resolution analysis. Here, we construct a spatiotemporal single-cell atlas of the silkworm wing disc across 10 time points, identifying 12 major cell types and their developmental transitions. Wing morphogenesis (Wm) cells act as central progenitors, differentiating into epithelial and cuticle lineages under lineage-specific transcription factors. Time‑resolved snRNA‑seq reveal hierarchical transcriptional reprogramming, with Wm cells functioning as early signaling hubs. Functional modules and signaling pathways were activated in spatiotemporal controlled manner. 20‑hydroxyecdysone treatment rapidly accelerates fate transitions and gene expression, recapitulating natural development within hours. Integration of morphology, hormone levels, and gene expression supports a five-stage Gene Transition Model describing progressive fate resolution. This work reveals wing development in silkworm and provides insights into hormone-driven organogenesis and potential manipulation of insect development in agriculture.

---

## Introduction

Insects are the only invertebrates that can fly, a key evolutionary innovation that allows them to travel long distances, escape predators, locate mates, and expand their foraging range. This ability has enabled insects to occupy diverse ecological niches and become the most species-rich group of animals on Earth1. Understanding how insect wings develop is thus fundamental to developmental biology and has practical value for pest control, evolutionary studies, and bio-inspired engineering. In holometabolous insects, their wings develop from specialized larval structures known as imaginal discs, particularly wing discs2. Wing discs are composed of diverse cell types that undergo continuous morphogenetic changes, ultimately forming the fully developed insect wing3,4. Knowing the spatial distribution and functional roles of these cells is important for understanding how wings form. Previous studies have shown that hormones and several signaling pathways play key roles in wing disc development5,6. Among them, 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) is the main hormone, driving the metamorphosis from larvae to adult stages by guiding cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis5,7. Meanwhile, classic pathways such as Hedgehog (Hh), Wnt, and Notch also play roles in cell fate, tissue organization, and organ formation8–10.

Although single-cell analyses have been conducted for the wing disc of Drosophila melanogaster (D. melanogaster) and Bicyclus anynana (B. anynana)11,12, they have mainly focused on cell type composition and gene expression patterns at isolated stages. These studies fail to capture the full continuum of cellular transitions across developmental time and often lack spatial resolution. Consequently, it remains unclear how different cell types interact, how their spatial arrangement evolves, and how they collectively respond to dynamic 20E signaling. A comprehensive, spatiotemporal view of wing disc development is imperative to fill these gaps.

The silkworm Bombyx mori (B. mori), is an important lepidopteran model of economic and developmental significance and serves as an ideal system for investigating developmental processes13,14. Bulk transcriptomic studies have identified temporal gene expression dynamics involving regulators such as BmBlimp-115, BmIGFLP16, BmChiNAG17, and BmSd18. However, these studies often focus on either temporal or spatial dimensions alone. Furthermore, bulk transcriptomic approaches average signals across heterogeneous tissues, lacking the resolution to uncover cell-type-specific dynamics or spatial regulatory cues. This makes it hard to understand how different cells change and interact within the tissue. Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomic technologies provide powerful tools to resolve cellular heterogeneity and gene expression dynamics at high resolution19–21. By integrating these approaches, it is possible to see how different cell types are arranged, how they develop over time, and how they communicate22–26.

In this work, we combined scRNA-seq, single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), and spatial transcriptomics (Stereo-seq) to construct a high-resolution spatiotemporal transcriptomic atlas of B. mori wing discs from larva to pupa. We systematically mapped the dynamics of 12 functional cell populations in wing disc and revealed molecular mechanisms underlying their differentiation trajectories, which are regulated by key transcription factors such as Rfx, Blimp-1, Dll, and Pur-alpha. Performing snRNA-seq on wing disc subjected to time-constrained 20E treatment, we discovered a “time-axis compression” effect. In this process, 20E caused rapid reprogramming of cell fates. Finally, we built a Gene Transition Model (GTM) explaining how cellular signal cascades respond to 20E levels changes to guide wing development. In summary, our work reveals the dynamic processes that build insect wings and provides new insights in studying wing development and lepidopteran pest insect’s control.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Liu etal. present a comprehensive multi-omics study that integrates scRNA-seq, snRNA-seq, and spatial transcriptomics to
construct a high-resolution spatiotemporal atlas of the Bombyx mori wing disc across multiple developmental stages. Based
on this resource, the authors propose a five-stage Gene Transition Model (GTM) regulated by 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) to
describe the temporal dynamics of cell fate reprogramming. This is an interesting and timely study that offers novel
insights into hormonal regulation during insect organogenesis and provides a theoretical framework for understanding genetic
control and potential molecular intervention strategies in Lepidoptera. In addition to its biological relevance, the dataset
represents a valuable resource for future research into wing disc development and
hormonal regulation. Overall the study is well performed and reads clearly. Prior to publications, I’d like to see some clarifications and revisions.
Main concerns:
1. In Fig. 3h, the comparison between naturally developing and 20E-induced samples could be expanded. It would be
valuable to clarify the similarities and differences in cell composition and pathway activity between the two conditions,
particularly considering how closely 20E treatment mimics natural developmental processes.
2. For Fig. S17, please provide functional enrichment results for the shared upregulated gene set between the natural and
20E-induced groups. This would help clarify the core biological processes directly regulated by 20E.
3. In Fig. 4h–i, the analysis of cell–cell interactions (CCI) does not clearly reflect stage-specific dynamics. The authors are
encouraged to highlight temporal shifts in interaction patterns across developmental stages.
4. The adult wing morphology following Rfx RNAi in Spodoptera frugiperda is not shown. Including representative images of
adult wing phenotypes would strengthen the phenotypic validation. Given its importance in supporting the evolutionary
conservation of Rfx, the S. frugiperda RNAi results should be moved to the main figures. Additionally, a comparative
analysis of Rfx conservation across insects would further support this claim.
5. Beyond Rfx, the authors are encouraged to functionally validate additional key transcription factors identified through
SCENIC analysis (e.g., Dll or Blimp-1) via RNAi or similar approaches.
6. In Fig. 3g, it would be helpful to indicate which cell types express the highlighted transcription factors and how their
activity contributes to cell-type-specific transcriptional regulation and heterogeneity.
7. The evolutionary comparison with Drosophila and B. anynana is relatively brief. A more detailed discussion of conserved
and lineage-specific developmental strategies across these species would enhance the impact of the comparative analysis.
8. While the methods section is generally well-detailed, additional clarification on the threshold settings and statistical
parameters used in transcription factor enrichment, module identification, and pathway analysis would improve transparency
and reproducibility.
Below are some minor comments for the authors to consider:
9. In Fig. 2j, the figure legend should specify “dsRfx” to match the experimental description. The labels in Fig. 3a–f should be
adjusted for better alignment, and the RSS values in Fig. 3j are too small to read clearly and should be enlarged.
10. Several supplementary figures appear to lack sufficient resolution. Please ensure all images are high-quality and include
appropriate legends and annotations for ease of interpretation.
11. Reference formatting should be carefully reviewed. Inconsistencies in journal name abbreviations and missing page
numbers should be corrected for uniformity.
12. In the author list, a comma should follow “Ying Lin” to maintain consistent punctuation.
13. Line 27: The full name of 20E should be written as “20-hydroxyecdysone”.
14. Line 90: “Fig. S1” should include a period to follow journal formatting guidelines.
15. Lines 105–106: The font style of reference citations appears inconsistent (non-italic). Please standardize formatting
across the manuscript.
16. Lines 180 and 185: The correct formatting should be “Fig. 2f and Fig. S7c”.

### Reviewer 2

The current manuscript outlines a spatial transcriptomic approach to map the development of wing discs in Bombyx mori.
The authors have compiled an impressive dataset, and undertaken extensive analysis, to identify the cell types within this
tissue, their spatial location, the changes in cell fates over time, and changes in gene expression that accompany these
changes. In addition, they explore how the steroid hormone ecdysone affects wing disc development, demonstrating that it
regulates the pace of wing disc development. We commend the authors on the scale of this work, and feel that it makes a
valuable contribution to our understanding of organ development. We have no experience with the transcriptomics
approaches used and thus will limit our comments to other aspects of the work, which we think would help strengthen the
manuscript.
The acronyms for the different cell types are really hard to keep track of. Can you use the whole word to make it easier to
follow?
The experiments knocking down Rfx in the wing disc were very interesting and highlighted the role of this gene in Wing
Morphogenesis cell type development. However, it wasn’t clear why this particular cell type was the focus?
This might sound a bit picky, but the order of the methods did not follow the order of experiments. This isn’t necessary, but
does help when trying to find the relevant method to match to the experiment.
For the wing disc culture experiments, more detail is required in the methods to understand how these were performed. What
medium did you use for culture and did you add any insulin or bovine serum? Preferably, this would have it’s own section.
For the experimental design, why did you choose to change the time of exposure instead of 20E dose? Lastly, 2µg / ml of
20E is a high dose for wing disc cultures. It would be useful to explain why you chose this dose.
Why were 20E titres collected from the wing discs and not from the hemolymph?
Some of the paragraphs were in really big blocks of text. It would help with readability to break up these paragraphs into
discrete ideas and to provide a bit more context throughout with regards to the aims of your different analyses.
Minor comments:

analogous)

are these different?

• In the text, you refer to 12 supplementary tables. These tables are found in the excel file. However, in the pdf there are only
3 supplementary tables and the formatting of these tables appears to be off.
• For Figure 3d (and the accompanying supplementary figure), it wasn’t clear what was meant by relative information flow.
• Figure S18: What do BF and Trans refer to?

Comment: 2. In Fig. 3h, the comparison between naturally developing and 20E-
induced samples could be expanded. It would be valuable to clarify the similarities and
differences in cell composition and pathway activity between the two conditions,
particularly considering how closely 20E treatment mimics natural developmental
processes.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. We agree
that a detailed comparison between natural development and 20E-induced conditions is
essential for evaluating the fidelity of the hormone induction system. To address this
point, we expanded our analyses of both cellular composition and pathway activity in
the revised manuscript.
At the cellular level, the major cell types captured in both conditions were similar.
However, their relative abundances and activation timings were different. During
natural development, the proportions of Wm, Cuticle, and Epithelial lineages changed
gradually from L5D1 to W1. In contrast, 20E treatment triggered a rapid and transient
expansion of these lineages within the first 30 min, followed by a pronounced shift
toward Matrix and Immune cell enrichment after 40 min. Notably, Matrix cells
exhibited a steady increase in both conditions (Fig. S18a).
At the transcriptional level, GO and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed distinct
functional states. Natural development (sc group) showed enrichment in Endocytosis,
mTOR signaling pathway, structural constituent of cuticle, and DNA-binding
transcription factor binding, reflecting sustained biosynthetic and morphogenetic
activity. Conversely, 20E-induced samples (sn group) were enriched in Ribosome
binding, mRNA binding, and Oxidative phosphorylation, indicating enhanced protein
synthesis, energy metabolism, and rapid transcriptional reprogramming (Fig. S18b–c).
These findings demonstrate that 20E treatment recapitulates the natural developmental
trajectory but in a time-compressed manner, accelerating lineage activation and
transcriptional remodeling. We have included these results in the revised manuscript
(Page 13, Lines 326–337) and added Supplementary Fig. S18 to clarify these
comparisons.
Comment: 3. For Fig. S17, please provide functional enrichment results for the shared
upregulated gene set between the natural and 20E-induced groups. This would help
clarify the core biological processes directly regulated by 20E.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. According to
your suggestion, we performed Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway enrichment
analyses on the 273 shared upregulated genes identified in both the natural development
and 20E-induced datasets. The enrichment results revealed that these shared genes are
significantly involved in developmental processes such as cellular morphogenesis,
organ growth, and tissue remodeling, as well as in stress and immune responses. In
addition, several pathways related to protein homeostasis and signal transduction—
including autophagy, MAPK signaling, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) protein
processing—were also enriched. These findings suggest that 20E regulates a core
transcriptional program that coordinates both structural remodeling and cellular stress
adaptation during wing disc development (Fig. S19b). We also analyzed the dynamic
expression patterns of these shared genes across natural development and 20E-treated
samples (Fig. S19c). The results showed a progressive, stage-specific activation from
L5D1 to P6 under natural development, transitioning sequentially from clusters C1 to
C10. Upon 20E treatment, many genes in clusters C3–C6 and C8–C10 responded
rapidly within 20 minutes, while genes in cluster C1, which were activated early during
natural development, were induced later under 20E exposure. These observations
provide a high-resolution view of 20E-induced transcriptional reprogramming and
underscore its role in accelerating developmental transitions within the wing disc. We
have incorporated these analyses into the revised Supplementary Figure S19 and
updated the corresponding description in the main text (Page 14, Lines 337–353). The
legend of Fig. S19 has also been revised accordingly.
Comment: 4. In Fig. 4h–i, the analysis of cell–cell interactions (CCI) does not clearly
reflect stage-specific dynamics. The authors are encouraged to highlight temporal shifts
in interaction patterns across developmental stages.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s careful work. We fully agree that highlighting
the stage-specific dynamics of cell–cell interactions (CCIs) would make the results
more intuitive. Accordingly, we revised and expanded the CCI analysis to better
illustrate temporal changes in intercellular communication across the five
developmental stages. In the revised version, we visualized the overall interaction
networks for each stage and emphasized their dynamic complexity (Fig. 4l). The cell-
cell interaction network gradually became more complex from Stage 1 to Stage 4 and
then simplified at Stage 5, indicating a transition from active remodeling to stabilization
(Fig. 4l). To improve clarity, we restructured Figs. 4m-n by highlighting the main
signaling sources with bold text and labeling each stage-specifically enriched
interactions with the corresponding stage label. This presentation makes the temporal
pattern of CCIs and the stage-specific signaling hubs easier to follow and interpret.
Please see Figure 4 for the revised visualization. The corresponding explanations have
been added to the main text of the revised manuscript (Page 17-19, Lines 414–448).
Comment: 5. The adult wing morphology following Rfx RNAi in Spodoptera

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important and constructive
suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have added representative images of the adult
wing phenotypes in S. frugiperda following Rfx RNAi to Figure 2 (Fig. 2o and Page
10, Line 231).
These images clearly display the morphological defects, such as shortened veins
and irregular wing margins, which support the functional disruption of Rfx. To highlight
the evolutionary conservation of Rfx, we have moved the Rfx RNAi knock down results
of S. frugiperda from the Supplementary Materials to the main figures (Fig. 2m–n).
Furthermore, to strengthen the evidence for evolutionary conservation, we
performed a comparative analysis of Rfx orthologs across representative insect species.
We constructed a phylogenetic tree using Rfx protein sequences from 23 representative
insect species and examined their motif organization and conserved domain
architecture. The analysis revealed that Rfx is highly conserved across Lepidoptera and
other insect lineages, suggesting a conserved regulatory function in wing development
(Fig. S10). Please see Supplementary Figure S10 below for the phylogenetic and motif
analyses. These new results and corresponding figure have been incorporated into the
revised manuscript (Supplementary Fig. S10 and Page 9, Lines 220–222). The
legends for Fig. 2 and Fig. S10 have also been updated accordingly.

Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. In the revised manuscript,
we have included additional functional validation experiments for key transcription
factors identified through the SCENIC analysis. Specifically, we focused on Distal-less
(Dll) and Pur-alpha, both predicted to play central roles in Wm cell differentiation and
wing disc development. RNAi-mediated knockdown of these genes in Bombyx mori
resulted in noticeable morphological defects in the wing disc, confirming their essential
regulatory roles in morphogenesis (Fig. S11). Please see Supplementary Figure S11
below. As for Blimp-1, previous studies have reported that RNAi-mediated knockdown
of Blimp-1 in Bombyx mori leads to disrupted wing development (Wu SY et al., 2019)1.
This literature evidence supports the functional importance of Blimp-1 identified in our
analysis and further exemplify the reliability of our transcription factor (TF) screening
strategy. Together, these results provide additional support for the functional relevance
of the key TFs identified by SCENIC. The new experimental results and related
references have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Fig. S11 and Page 9,
Lines 225–228).

Comment: 7. In Fig. 3g, it would be helpful to indicate which cell types express the
highlighted transcription factors and how their activity contributes to cell-type-specific
transcriptional regulation and heterogeneity.
Response: We thank the reviewers for pointing out this issue. According to your
suggestion, we have provided the cell-type–specific expression patterns and temporal
activities of the transcription factors in Supplementary Figure S16a. Based on regulon
specificity scores (RSS) and expression dynamics across developmental stages, we
identified six key TFs that exhibit distinct temporal activation patterns and cell-type
preferences. In the early stage (before 30 min), Hr38 (LOC693064), Nubbin
(LOC101744796), and Six2 (LOC101735990) showed strong activity, regulating gene
networks enriched in Wm, Epithelial 1, and Cuticle 1 cells. After 30 min, CREB
(LOC692871), FoxN3 (LOC101739133), and GATA-A (LOC10174013) became
predominant, with activities mainly associated with Immune and Matrix cells. These
findings suggest a temporal transition of TF activity from early patterning factors to
regulators of morphogenesis and tissue remodeling. We have incorporated these
analyses and explanatory descriptions into the revised manuscript (Figs. 3g and S16,
Page 12, Lines 304–312), and the legends of Fig. 3g and Fig. S16 have been updated
accordingly.
Comment: 8. The evolutionary comparison with Drosophila and B. anynana is
relatively brief. A more detailed discussion of conserved and lineage-specific
developmental strategies across these species would enhance the impact of the
comparative analysis.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree
that a deeper evolutionary perspective would enhance the impact of our comparative
analysis. Comparing our findings in B. mori with that of D. melanogaster and B.
anynana revealed both conserved regulatory modules and lineage-specific
developmental strategies (Fig. S23a and b). Core pathways such as Wnt, Notch, and
MAPK were consistently involved in cell fate determination and tissue patterning
across species. However, our findings highlight several specific adaptations in B. mori.
Specifically, the Wm cell in B. mori followed a bifurcated developmental trajectory
toward epithelial and cuticle fates. This distinct progenitor identity has not been clearly
reported in Drosophila, suggesting a silkworm-specific mechanism for lineage
allocation. In B. anynana, a more diversified set of scale precursor cells supports
elaborate wing coloration and patterning, highlighting another lineage-specific
adaptation (Fig. S23c). Furthermore, although 20E functions as a conserved hormone
regulating metamorphosis, our data point to a silkworm-specific mode of spatial and
temporal hormone responsiveness. In B. mori, Wm cells responded rapidly and locally
to 20E, initiating early morphogenetic programs. This contrasts with the more systemic
and less spatially resolved 20E response observed in Drosophila. Taken together, these
comparisons demonstrate that while fundamental signaling frameworks are preserved,
each lineage has evolved tailored regulatory strategies—shaped by ecological pressures
and morphogenetic needs. Our single-cell and spatial atlas of B. mori not only confirms
these shared principles but also provides a valuable reference for exploring how
evolutionary flexibility in hormone integration and progenitor dynamics contributes to
wing diversity in insects. We have expanded the Discussion section to include this
detailed comparison in the revised manuscript (Pages 23-24, Lines 554–572).
Comment: 9. While the methods section is generally well-detailed, additional

Response: We thank the reviewer's careful work. We have thoroughly gone through the

Response: We thank the reviewers for pointing out this issue. We fully understand that

In our study, due to the large number of cell types identified through single-cell

Comment: 3. The experiments knocking down Rfx in the wing disc were very
interesting and highlighted the role of this gene in Wing Morphogenesis cell type
development. However, it wasn’t clear why this particular cell type was the focus?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful question. Our focus on
the Wing Morphogenesis (Wm) cell type was based on several layers of observations
during wing disc (WD) development.
First, when examining the dynamic changes in the proportion and differentiation
trajectory of cell types across developmental stages, we observed that most cell types
in the WD maintained a relatively stable state and did not exhibit significant lineage
progression (as shown in Fig. S6a–f). In contrast, Wm cells demonstrated a markedly
dynamic and continuous differentiation trajectory, with clear transitions toward cuticle
and epithelial (EP) lineages (Fig. S6g). This suggests that Wm cells are a pivotal cell
type in the developmental progression of the wing disc. Second, spatial transcriptomics
data further corroborated this finding. We identified Wm cells as being specifically
enriched in the wing bud region, the future wing-forming domain of the WD (Fig. 1g–
h). This spatial localization aligns with their predicted role in driving the formation of
wing-specific structures. Motivated by the above observations, we sought to uncover
potential transcriptional regulators specifically involved in wing disc cell fate decisions.
Through the reconstruction of a transcription factor regulatory network and RSS
scoring, we found that Rfx emerged as the top-ranked specific transcription factor at
the L5D1 stage. Which leading us to hypothesize that Rfx may serve as a core regulator
in Wm cell lineage commitment.
To validate this hypothesis, we performed RNAi-mediated knockdown of Rfx and
observed striking disruptions in wing disc morphology and gene expression associated
with Wm-derived lineages (Fig. 2j–l and Fig. S9), confirming its critical role in
modulating Wm cell fate and wing development.

Comment: 5. For the wing disc culture experiments, more detail is required in the
methods to understand how these were performed. What medium did you use for
culture and did you add any insulin or bovine serum? Preferably, this would have it’s
own section. For the experimental design, why did you choose to change the time of
exposure instead of 20E dose? Lastly, 2µg / ml of 20E is a high dose for wing disc
cultures. It would be useful to explain why you chose this dose.
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. We have added a dedicated
section in the Methods to comprehensively describe the in vitro wing disc culture and
20E treatment experiments. Specifically, the wing discs were cultured in Grace’s
medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum.
Regarding the experimental design, we chose to vary the duration of 20E exposure
rather than its concentration. This decision was based on two main considerations. First,
due to the open circulatory system of Bombyx mori, endogenous 20E levels in the
hemolymph can influence multiple tissues simultaneously. Second, the permeability
and uptake efficiency of exogenous 20E by the wing disc in vitro is unclear. This
approach allowed us to capture the temporal sequence of gene activation in response to
20E and to compare it with the natural developmental timeline.
To ensure a robust and consistent hormonal response will be induced in cultured
wing discs, we performed a preliminary dose-response experiment to select optimized
concentration for 20E. Wing discs were cultured with various concentrations of 20E (0,
0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, and 10 μg/mL) and relative expression of key 20E responsive genes
were measured using quantitative PCR. We found that at 2 µg/mL, the transcriptional
levels of EcR and USP, were markedly induced (Fig. S13a). This concentration is also
supported by previous studies reporting effective hormonal stimulation at similar levels
in cultured wing discs (Ali et al., 2019)1. Hence, we used 2 µg/mL 20E to stimulate
wing disc in vitro to investigate gene expression dynamics. All these details have been
incorporated into the revised Methods section (Page 11 lines 266–269 and pages 28-
29 lines 707–730).

Comment: 6. Why were 20E titres collected from the wing discs and not from the
hemolymph?
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful question. We chose to analyze 20E titers
directly from the wing discs (WDs) rather than the hemolymph for the following
reasons. First, the dynamic changes of 20E concentration in the hemolymph during
silkworm development have already been well documented in previous studies. Second,
the silkworm possesses an open circulatory system, and 20E in the hemolymph is
distributed to various tissues and organs, not exclusively acting on the wing discs.
Therefore, measuring 20E in the hemolymph would not provide precise information
about the local hormonal milieu experienced by the developing WDs. Our goal was to
investigate the tissue-specific 20E dynamics during wing morphogenesis, and thus we
directly measured the hormone levels in the WDs. We have clarified this rationale in
the Method section of revised manuscript to improve transparency (Page 30, line 774–
778).

Comment: 11. Line 242: You mention Usp is expressed in Wm cells, but EcR isn’t in

Response: We thank the reviewer’s careful work. We found that EcR gene expression

expression was sufficiently robust to be captured during the experiment, whereas EcR
may have been underrepresented due to such stochastic dropout effects.
